research_question: Does robust contrastive responsibility require irreducibly de se representation of the selected outcome, or only representation of that outcome as resulting from an act the agent performs or selects?

argument.title: Self-Location Constraint
argument.paper_title: God and the View From Nowhere: De Se Knowledge and Divine Omniscience

premises.text: If an agent is robustly responsible for bringing about one outcome rather than another, its cognition must represent the first outcome as its own action.
premises.quote: If an agent is robustly responsible for bringing about φ rather than ψ, then the agent’s cognitive state must represent φ as the outcome of its own action rather than ψ.

premises.text: Robust contrastive responsibility requires cognition that represents an outcome as issuing from the agent's own activity rather than relevant alternatives.
premises.quote: where responsibility is understood contrastively, the cognitive state constitutive of responsible agency must itself represent the relevant outcome as issuing from the agent’s own activity rather than the relevant alternatives.

premises.text: A third-personal proposition identifying God as actualising a world does not itself represent that actualisation under the first-personal aspect required for source attribution.
premises.quote: A third-personal proposition such as “God actualises W1” may identify the correct agent extensionally, yet it does not by itself represent the actualisation under the first-personal aspect required for source attribution.

premises.text: Robust contrastive responsibility requires divine cognition to represent God as the source of actualising W1 rather than W0.
premises.quote: The relevant question is not merely which world becomes actual, but whether divine cognition represents God as the source of actualising W1 rather than W0.

missing_premise.text: God's contrastive responsibility for actualising one world rather than another is robust responsibility, and representing God as the source of that actualisation requires irreducible de se content.

conclusion.text: If God is contrastively responsible for actualising one world rather than another, divine cognition must include irreducible de se content.

challenged_premise.text: If an agent is robustly responsible for bringing about one outcome rather than another, its cognition must represent the first outcome as its own action.

objection: Ines, a reservoir controller, faces rising water during a storm. Opening the east spillway will flood farmland; doing nothing will let the dam overtop and flood the town. She studies hydrographs, weighs crop losses against lives, and concludes, in exactly these terms, 'The farmland should flood rather than the town.' She opens the spillway and the farmland floods. The inquiry finds her robustly responsible for the farmland flooding rather than the town: she foresaw it, compared it with the alternative, chose it knowingly, and could have done otherwise. Yet the outcome she represented, the farmland under water, was never represented as her action. It is a hydrological event downstream, and she represented it as one. The only thing she represented as her doing was turning the spillway wheel, and that is a different item from the outcome for which she is held responsible. Her responsibility for the flood rests on representing the flood as a foreseen consequence she was choosing between, not on representing the flood as her action.

strongest_responses.response: The objector is right that the distal outcome need not be represented as the agent's action. Responsibility instead requires representing the selected outcome, under the relevant contrast, as the result of an act the agent performs and intends.
strongest_responses.why_it_failed: This concedes the challenged premise as stated. The revision may preserve the wider argument, but it requires a further case that representing an act of actualising as one's own entails irreducible de se content in the divine case.

strongest_responses.response: The relevant source-attribution condition attaches to the act-outcome relation: the agent represents that, by performing a selected intervention, the outcome will result. A merely third-personal identification of an actualised world may still omit the first-personal standpoint of selecting it.
strongest_responses.why_it_failed: The reply successfully distinguishes the outcome from the action and retains an agent-relative condition. It does not establish that this condition cannot be met by non-de-se, third-personal divine cognition, especially if God can represent an act as God's own without irreducible first-personal content.

nearest.title: Compassion, Doubt, and Eternal Damnation: An Analysis of Sincere Belief and Doubt Under Religious Diversity — 31

open_questions: Is representing an outcome as issuing from an act one performs sufficient for robust contrastive responsibility, or must the agent also intend the outcome rather than merely foresee it?
Does source attribution to an act require irreducible de se content, or can it be expressed through a suitably rich third-personal proposition?
What distinguishes divine actualisation from ordinary cases in which an agent represents a distal consequence as resulting from a chosen intervention?
Does the revised premise support the original conclusion about divine cognition without adding substantive premises about intention, agency, or self-ascription?
paper_direction: A paper here would argue that the objection identifies a genuine equivocation between responsibility for an outcome and representing that outcome as an action: robust contrastive responsibility requires an agent-relative representation of the act–outcome relation, not self-representation of the distal outcome as an action. The case would develop the reservoir example and analogous ordinary agency cases, then anticipate the strongest reply that source attribution still requires a first-personal stance toward the selected act. It would need to show either that this stance is available in non-de-se terms, weakening the route to the divine conclusion, or that a principled feature of divine actualisation makes irreducible de se content necessary despite the revised premise.

reasons.coherence: The objection is internally consistent and does falsify c005 read literally, but it aims at a phrasing the surrounding premises (c006, c008) make clear was not the operative claim.
reasons.robustness: The obvious repair ('represent the outcome as resulting from one's own act') is conceded by the direction itself, and the case presupposes a causal gap that divine basic action plausibly lacks; neither the plan nor the transcript answers this.
reasons.significance: Success would yield a wording fix to one premise while leaving the de se inference intact, since the revised condition is still agent-relative and the Ines case is itself de se; the substantive question is only gestured at in the open questions.
reasons.specificity: There is a definite thesis and a worked case, but the decisive second stage is posed as an unresolved disjunction ('either available in non-de-se terms, or divine actualisation makes it necessary'), with no plan for settling it.

assessment.strongest_objection: The objection exploits loose wording rather than a substantive commitment. The argument's own c006 and c008 already state the real condition: representing the outcome as issuing from the agent's activity, with first-personal source attribution. Swapping 'as its own action' for 'as resulting from its own action' repairs c005 at no cost. And in the divine case the act–outcome gap the Ines case relies on collapses, because actualising a world is plausibly a basic action with no intervening causal chain. Worse, Ines's own representation ('by my opening the spillway, the farmland floods') is itself de se. So the case leaves the inference to irreducible de se content untouched.
assessment.what_it_needs: The paper must drop the outcome/action equivocation as its main contribution. It should argue directly that agent-relative source attribution can be met by non-de-se content, engaging the Perry/Lewis/Castañeda literature and the Kretzmann/Grim debates on omniscience and indexicals. It must also address why divine actualisation, which lacks a proximal/distal gap, does not simply restore the original premise.
assessment.summary: A clean counterexample to a carelessly worded premise, but it is easily repaired and does not reach the de se issue, so it would be dismissed as verbal unless rebuilt around whether source attribution can be non-de-se.

revision.research_question: Does robust contrastive responsibility require irreducibly de se representation of the selected outcome, or is agent-relative source attribution, represented in non-de-se terms, enough; and does divine basic action change that answer?
revision.paper_direction: A paper here would argue that the premise as literally stated, that the outcome must be represented as the agent's own action, is false, as the reservoir case shows. It would then argue that the repaired condition, that cognition represent the outcome as resulting from the agent's own act, is agent-relative but can in ordinary agency be met by non-de-se content: the agent describes the act-outcome link in general terms and identifies her own act de re through a perceptually given candidate, the spillway wheel she turns. The paper would then argue that the divine case removes that anchor, since actualising a world is not given among candidate acts and has no proximal/distal gap. It would test the two remaining routes. On the first, God knows de re that God actualises W1, which is non-de-se if God's self-identification is secured without a further self-locating fact. On the second, source attribution requires a first-personal identification of the act as one's own when no other anchor is available, which would make de se content irreducible. The paper would defend a conditional verdict: the divine conclusion holds only if basic actualisation is selected among alternatives and no non-indexical means of identifying it as God's own act is available. It would engage the Perry, Lewis and Castañeda literature on essential indexicals and the Kretzmann and Grim debates on omniscience and indexicals to decide whether that condition is met.
revision.reply_to_strongest_objection: The paper accepts the referee's point that 'resulting from its own action' repairs the premise at no cost, so the outcome/action equivocation is not its main contribution. It also accepts that Ines's own report is de se at the act level. It replies on two fronts. First, it distinguishes self-ascribing the property of being the actualiser from identifying oneself de re under a name or essence; the repaired premise requires only the former if the latter can secure source attribution. Second, it grants that basic action removes the proximal/distal gap, but argues this does not remove the need to identify which act is one's own. The paper therefore tests whether that identification can be non-indexical in the divine case, rather than assuming it.
revision.what_changed: The revision drops the outcome/action equivocation as the main contribution, concedes that the literal premise is false and its repair is cheap, and makes the divine de se conclusion conditional on whether non-indexical identification of basic actualisation as God's own act is available.

reasons.coherence: The objection is internally consistent and does falsify c005 as literally stated, but it is loosely aimed, since c006 and c031 already express the source condition it leaves untouched, and the paper's distinction between self-ascription and de re identification is muddled.
reasons.robustness: The obvious reply is that the counterexample is an equivocation repaired by premises already in the argument; the direction concedes this, and its substantive fallback rests on a confused contrast, so no viable answer is yet in hand.
reasons.significance: If the conditional verdict were secured with a clear account of non-indexical self-identification in basic divine action, it would usefully refine the omniscience-and-indexicals debate, but it would not reshape it.
reasons.specificity: The plan is concrete: concede the literal point, separate the anchored ordinary case from basic actualisation, test two named routes, and reach a conditional verdict against a specified literature, although the criterion for 'no non-indexical means available' is left undefined.

assessment.strongest_objection: The reservoir case refutes only a careless wording of c005. The argument already contains the intended condition in c006 and c031: representing the outcome as issuing from the agent's own activity. So the counterexample is idle against the argument. Once the paper concedes this, as it does, what remains is the familiar Kretzmann/Grim/Castañeda question of whether God can know 'I am actualising W1' without irreducible indexical content. The paper's first reply also seems to concede that question rather than answer it. On the Lewisian view, self-ascribing the property of being the actualiser simply is de se content. So the proposed contrast between self-ascription and de re self-identification under a name or essence cannot do the work assigned to it.
assessment.what_it_needs: Drop the reservoir counterexample as the lead and target c006/c031 directly. Then state precisely what a non-indexical, non-self-ascriptive identification of an act as God's own would be. A promising route is that a necessarily unique actualiser faces no self-locating uncertainty, so de se and de re content may coincide in God's case. The paper must show how this advances beyond Kretzmann, Castañeda and Grim.
assessment.summary: The headline counterexample is a wording point that the argument's other premises already fix, and the real project is a reworking of the old omniscience-and-indexicals debate that still needs a coherent account of non-de-se self-identification before it is a paper.
